question: The altitude to the hypotenuse of a \(30\)-\(60\)-\(90^\circ\) right triangle is divided into two segments of lengths \(x \lt y\) by the median to the shortest side of the triangle. What is the ratio \(\dfrac{x}{x + y}?\)
solution:
The median creates equal areas, and area ratios can then reveal how it divides the altitude.

Let \(C\) be the right-angle vertex of triangle \(ABC\), with \(BC\) the shortest side. Let \(H\) be the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to hypotenuse \(AB\). Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(BC\), and let \(P\) be the intersection of median \(AM\) with altitude \(CH\).

Scale the triangle so that \(BC=1\). Since the shortest leg of a \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle is half its hypotenuse, \(AB=2\).

Triangles \(BHC\) and \(BCA\) are similar: both are right triangles and they share the angle at \(B\). Matching corresponding sides gives
\[
\frac{BH}{BC}=\frac{BC}{BA},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad BH=\frac12.
\]
Hence \(AH=2-\frac12=\frac32\), and \(AH/AB=3/4\).

Write \([UVW]\) for the area of triangle \(UVW\). Because \(BM=CM\), triangles \(ABM\) and \(ACM\) have equal areas: they have equal bases on \(BC\) and a common height from \(A\). Similarly, \([PBM]=[PCM]\). Subtracting these smaller areas gives
\[
[ABP]=[ACP].
\]
Triangles \(AHP\) and \(ACP\) have bases \(HP\) and \(CP\) on the same line \(CH\), so their area ratio is \(HP/CP\). Triangles \(AHP\) and \(ABP\) have bases \(AH\) and \(AB\) on the same line, so their area ratio is \(AH/AB\). Thus
\[
\frac{HP}{CP}
=\frac{[AHP]}{[ACP]}
=\frac{[AHP]}{[ABP]}
=\frac{AH}{AB}
=\frac34.
\]
Therefore \(HP\) is the shorter segment. Since \(CH=HP+CP\), the requested fraction is
\[
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{HP}{CH}=\boxed{\frac{3}{7}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Placing the legs on coordinate axes turns the altitude and median into simple line equations.

The \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) side ratio is \(1:\sqrt3:2\). Choose coordinates
\[
C=(0,0),\qquad B=(1,0),\qquad A=(0,\sqrt3),
\]
so \(C\) is the right-angle vertex and \(BC\) is the shortest side. Its midpoint is \(M=(1/2,0)\).

Use \((u,v)\) for coordinates, keeping \(x,y\) for the segment lengths in the question. The hypotenuse \(AB\) has equation
\[
v=\sqrt3(1-u).
\]
Its slope is \(-\sqrt3\). Perpendicular nonvertical lines have slopes whose product is \(-1\), so the altitude from \(C\) has equation
\[
v=\frac{u}{\sqrt3}.
\]
At its foot \(H\) on \(AB\),
\[
\frac{u}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3(1-u)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=3(1-u).
\]
Thus \(H=(3/4,\sqrt3/4)\).

The median \(AM\) has slope \(-2\sqrt3\), hence equation
\[
v=\sqrt3(1-2u).
\]
At its intersection \(P\) with the altitude,
\[
\frac{u}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3(1-2u)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=3(1-2u).
\]
Therefore \(P=(3/7,\sqrt3/7)\), which lies between \(C\) and \(H\).

The distance formula gives
\[
CH=\sqrt{\frac9{16}+\frac3{16}}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2},
\qquad
CP=\sqrt{\frac9{49}+\frac3{49}}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{7}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{CP}{CH}=\frac47,
\qquad
\frac{PH}{CH}=1-\frac47=\frac37.
\]
Since \(PH\) is shorter, \(x=PH\), and
\[
\frac{x}{x+y}=\boxed{\frac37},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Find the intersections with coordinates
